work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: De centurione et contra Manichaeos et Apolinaristas

paragraphs.text: The clouds have whitened the earth with snow, and the snowflakes of the holy Scriptures whiten our souls with the divine word. For they make their way into our souls, these divine snowflakes, like rain upon the grass and like snow upon the pasture, and they both water us and make us white. They water us so that we bear the fruits of godliness, and they make us white by cleansing away the filth of sin. For whoever is washed by the divine word is shown to be whiter than snow, as David said: “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.” Our soul is made white both by the divine doctrines and by the moral precepts. Faith, which enlightens our mind, must come first, and works, which make the soul shine, must follow. Faith comes before everything, and in today’s reading the Saviour marvelled at it, saying: “Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

The centurion grasped the dignity of the one who worked the miracles; he asked the Saviour for a command and recognized his sovereign authority. The heretics, though they read the Law and the Prophets, the Gospels and the apostles, have failed to recognize his dignity and have insulted the power of the Only-begotten, saying that he is subject to the Father’s authority. They do not know that the power belongs in common to the divine essence and that its authority is undivided: “For I and the Father are one.” But let us return to our subject. That admirable centurion says: “Say the word, and my servant will be healed. There is no need for you to come in body. The divine power is everywhere; it is not confined by place but encompasses all things by the divine Spirit. The Jews invite you into a house because they do not know your dignity. But I know that you are present everywhere, that you command by a word and accomplish all things with a nod. I have appealed to you as Master; I appeal to you also as God. I entreat you as Saviour and I plead with you as benefactor. My servant lies at home terribly ill, in torment.”

And see how firm the faithful man’s mind is. He did not come in person but through the elders, not because he was trying to get out of making the request, but because he considered himself unworthy to see the Saviour face to face. For he says: “I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. That is why I did not think myself worthy to come to you.” Beautiful is the faithful man’s modesty: out of reverence he declines to see him face to face, yet he proclaims his dignity with a true word. The elders of the Jews came, elders of little faith pleading for a faithful servant. The rulers of the synagogue were saying, “Come and heal him.” But he, having sent the delegation and recognized his dignity, says: “Do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you enter my house.” — “And where have you had experience of my word?”

“I know that you are God from your miracles. And the word of God creates nature and sets it right, and is the foundation of all things that appear. Say the word, for ‘by your word the heavens were made firm.’ Say the word, for by a word you laid the foundations of the earth, by a word you made the heavens firm, by a word you set bounds to the sea, by a word you set all things in order. You give commands to all your creatures: ‘You send forth the light and it goes; you call it, and it obeys you with trembling,’ as Jeremiah says. ‘And the stars shine for you with gladness. You called them, and they said, “Here we are.”’ You give orders to the visible creation and command the creation above the world, and can you not drive away diseases by the same command? Say the word. I need a word from God the Word. Say the word, and my servant will be healed.” Now we must understand that there is a great difference in the matter of faith, and how — listen, brother: there are some who reach the summit of faith, others who have a middling faith, others who are of little faith, still others who are doubtful in faith, and again others who are faithless.

Those who are faithful in the highest degree are wonderful, like this centurion, to whom the Saviour bore witness when he said, “Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith,” and like that Canaanite woman who came to him, at whom the Lord marvelled and said, “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.” These, then, are the supremely faithful. The faithless are those wholly cut off from godliness. The doubtful are those who stand on the border between faith and unbelief, who sometimes assent to the word and sometimes reject it. The Gospel once accuses the Saviour’s disciples of this kind of doubtfulness, before they were made perfect. For when it was announced to them that the Lord had risen from the dead, “some,” it says, “believed, but some doubted.” To doubt, to stand with a divided heart, to believe and disbelieve at once — this is often what happens to the souls of many when they think about Christ. For when we take on the heretics, our listeners sometimes assent to the dignity of the Only-begotten, but at other times their minds are shaken by the heretics’ words and they find themselves in doubt, now looking to the glory of Christ, now leaning toward heretical wickedness.

But God used to rebuke such little faith. For faith of this kind falls short and is deficient. It is possible to believe and yet to believe deficiently. That is why the apostle, knowing that there is a faith that is deficient and lacking, says to the Romans: “so that when I come I may supply what is lacking in your faith” [sic]. So it is possible both to believe and to fall short of the summit of faith. Little faith, then, means thinking something small about God, as when the Saviour reproached Peter, who went out onto the sea, walked in faith, and afterwards doubted. That is why he says to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” He did not say “Faithless one,” but “You of little faith,” for Peter had shown a little faith. At first, when he saw the Saviour walking on the sea, and the sea spreading its waves beneath him and laying out its back for the Master’s steps, he recalled the saying of David: “Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps will not be known.” And he said to his Saviour: “Lord, if it is you, let me come to you on the waters.”

The Master permitted it, the servant followed, and a man stepped onto the back of the sea. Then the sea stirred up its waves — or rather, a violent wind fell upon the waters, churned up the waves of the sea and troubled its whole surface. The servant was shaken and began to sink. It was not his body that was first in danger; he was submerged by little faith. He saw the sea raging and the winds in turmoil, and, falling away from his earlier faith, he was about to go under. And he calls to the Saviour: “Lord, help me.” And Jesus says to him: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” Yet not even the first part was a matter of unbelief. To say, “If it is you, command me to come to you on the waters,” was the act of one who recognized the dignity of the one giving the command; and, while sinking, not to look to anyone else but to seek help from him and to say, “Lord, help,” was the act not of one who disbelieves but of one who believes. So the Gospel finds fault with him not because he called on the Master, but because he thought he was sinking while the Master was right there.

“Why,” he says, “after my permission, after my nod, were you afraid of the sea? I gave you leave, saying, ‘Come,’ and did you think the wind was stronger than my command? Did the wind frighten you, as though it were stronger than my nod? Am I not the one who walks on the wings of the winds? Or does the sea alarm you? I am the one who rebukes the sea and dries it up. Why then do you fear the creation when the Creator is present?” But perhaps Peter will say: “Why then, Lord, did the sea dare to rebel while you were present? Why did it raise its waves while you were present?” The sea rebelled, Peter, not out of contempt for Christ, but to test you. For the sea was always a tutor correcting the unbelief of the disciples.

On that other occasion the Saviour went out on the sea; he went not walking but sailing. For when he wishes, he makes his dignity known, and when he wishes, he fulfils the plan of his incarnation. He walked on the sea as on dry ground; he got into a boat as a man. And he not only boarded the boat, he even slept in the boat. Did the nature that never sleeps sleep in a boat? He who lulls the waves to sleep slept in a boat — he of whom the prophet said, “Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.” He got in and slept, and again the sea raised its waves, not out of contempt for the Master, but to expose the little faith of the disciples — I mean the little faith they had before they were made perfect. Let no one take offence at what I say. I am not accusing the apostles; I am exposing the apostles’ weakness, so that afterwards you may recognize the apostles’ power. Simon the fisherman is one thing, Peter the apostle another; Matthew the tax collector is one thing, Matthew the evangelist another.

First recognize the lowliness of the fishermen, and then marvel at the magnificence of the apostles. The sea raises its waves. They were in danger and tossed by the storm. And he who rebukes the sea was there, and did not rebuke it. For he knew that it was training the disciples in danger like a good tutor. In that state, then, they saw him as a man sleeping, and they appealed to him as a man, saying: “Master, Master, get up, save us, we are perishing!” You call him “Master,” as one calls a teacher? That is why the sea is angry; that is why it rebels against you: because you do not yet recognize the Lord, but call him a teacher, saying, “Master.” So either tone down your words, or I will not calm the waves. “Master, we are perishing!” The one called “Master” rises and shows himself to be Lord. And what does he say to them? “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” See how everywhere he rebukes whoever does not recognize his dignity. “Why do you call me a mere master?” — “I saw you sleeping,” he says, “and I came to you as to a man.” — “Then, because you saw me sleeping, you failed to recognize the dignity that never sleeps. Could you not say, as David did, ‘Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord?’ Why did you not call me Lord, instead of ‘Master,’ like an ordinary teacher? If you call me a teacher, are you looking for help? What teacher can lull the waves to sleep? What teacher can rebuke a storm at sea? If you think me a teacher, let the teacher sleep. But if you call on God, recognize his dignity and receive his help.”

But he rebukes them for their little faith, and he commands the sea by his sovereign authority. He says to the sea: “Be silent! Be still!” No sooner had the word gone forth than the sea recognized the command. It was ordered to be silent, and it fell silent. It was ordered to be calm, and it did not talk back. It was this, I think, that blessed David was prefiguring — or rather foretelling — when he said in the hundred and sixth psalm, sketching the image of the apostles and the storm on the sea: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do their work on many waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.” Sometimes one of our opponents carries off a listener by saying: “David is describing the wonders at the Red Sea, which the Israelites saw as they walked on foot through the deep, when the waters were frozen into a wall, when Pharaoh was drowned and Israel was saved. It was then,” he says, “that those who went down saw the wonders in the deep.” But the opening words refute them. For the children of Israel went in on foot, whereas here he speaks not of those who walk but of those who sail. That is why he says: “Those who go down to the sea in ships.” And “those who do their work” means nothing other than the craft of fishermen. “Those who do their work on many waters” — that is, the fishermen — “they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.”

What wonders? “He spoke, and the stormy wind arose.” Here he shows that the sea was stirred up at God’s command. For it would not have raged against the disciples if the Master had not willed it. “Its waves were lifted high.” And the apostles — what of them? “They were troubled, they staggered like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.” What wisdom? Faith. Their wisdom was swallowed up, overpowered by little faith, “and they cried out to the Lord in their distress”: “Master, Master, we are perishing!” “And he saved them for his name’s sake.” And what came after that? That command of the Gospel: “Be silent! Be still!” See how the prophet foretells it: “And he rebuked the storm, and it subsided into a breeze, and its waves fell silent.” So he rebukes the sea, and it grows quiet. It recognized the Master’s command and is calm. He rebuked it in order to calm it; he did not threaten it, so as not to dry it up. For if he had threatened it, he would have dried it up, as the prophet says: “He threatens the sea and dries it up.”

Then, after the rebuke, the disciples begin to say: “Who is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” See how they still did not recognize his dignity, because they were attending to his human condition. Then what does the Gospel add? “Some of the disciples in the boat,” it says, “came and worshipped him, saying, ‘Truly you are the Son of God.’” See how the sea helped them. Before the storm they called him “Master”; after the storm they confessed him Son of God. The storm revealed his dignity: “Truly you are the Son of God.” All this I have said to show the distinction between faith, unbelief, little faith and doubtful faith. Now the Saviour, extolling the centurion as godlike for saying, “Say the word, and my servant will be healed,” says to those following him: “Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

Did you not find faith in Israel? Were you not asked to lay your hand on Peter’s mother-in-law? If they did not believe, how could they have asked? But he did not say, “I have not found,” but, “I have not found such faith.” “I was asked to lay my hand on Peter’s mother-in-law, but no one was as clear-headed as this man, to say: ‘Say the word and drive away the fever.’ Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, also called on me and said to me: ‘My little daughter is dying; come and heal her.’ And when I had said to him, ‘Take heart, your daughter lives,’ he said, ‘Lord, come before she dies.’ He did not recognize the dignity of my word, but demanded the presence of my body. Many have believed, but not like this man; they believed, but not as he did. Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

This faithful man, then, brought forth faith out of a good treasure, while the heretic brings forth unbelief out of an evil treasure. And see the understanding of Scripture — or rather, see the fountain of wisdom and what it says: “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings forth evil things.” Notice here how he pointed not to a nature that is evil or good, but to free choice, which can incline toward this or look toward that. This saying refutes the wickedness of the Manichaeans, who define the flesh as evil and the soul as coming from the good. For the children of the Manichaeans hold that the flesh belongs to the evil one, that is, to the devil, and the soul to God.

But the divine Scripture refutes them. For if the heart belongs to the body, how does it bring forth good things out of the evil treasure? What is evil by nature cannot bring forth good things. Let them define it however they like, then. They want our heart to be evil: why then does it bring forth good things? Or is it good by nature? Then why does it bring forth evil? And so you discover how rotten their unbelief is. That is why he set down both, and spoke of an evil man and a good man, so that you would not disparage nature but would recognize free choice. “The good man” first — see how he gives a good nature, or rather a good name: “the good man” and “the evil man.” If he is evil by nature, why is he good? And if he is good by nature, why is he evil? See how he is not now discussing nature, but defining the power of free choice.

But the Manichaeans bring forward the apostle and slander the apostolic voice, claiming it says that the flesh is evil. “Listen,” they say, “to what Paul teaches: ‘Now the works of the flesh are plain: they are fornication, adultery’ and so on. ‘But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace’ and so on. Do you see,” they say, “how he sets flesh and spirit against each other, and calls the one a source of good things and the other a source of evil?” Let us see, then, whether the apostle’s words really agree with their wickedness, rather than explaining the power of free choice. If the flesh is an evil creation and the work of the evil one, why do good things come into being through the evil flesh? If the tongue were evil by nature, it ought not to speak about God. The tongue ought not to say anything auspicious. The tongue ought to shun divine things altogether as foreign to it, and only speak obscenities and blasphemies and do everything proper to the flesh. How then does teaching about holiness come through the tongue, if it is by nature a thing of evil?

And why does the word of God make its way through these ears, which on their view are instruments of the devil? If the instrument is alien, how does it receive the working of the good? Why do the eyes, if they are of the evil nature, look upward to the one who dwells in heaven? If the mouth belongs to the evil one, why does the prophet say, “My mouth shall speak wisdom”? For wisdom is foreign to wickedness. If the hands are an evil instrument, why do they do works of mercy? Why are they spread out to God? “For I stretch out my hands to God Most High, who made heaven and earth.” If this belly that receives food were a construction of the evil one, why does it receive the law within it? “To do your will, O God,” it says, “I have desired, and your law is within my belly.” If the feet are a part of the evil one, why do they worship? For the bending of the knee in worship is accomplished by means of the feet. And why does David say, “My foot has stood on level ground”? If it belongs to wickedness, how does it know uprightness? Let these points refute the impiety of the heretics.

What then does Paul mean when he says, “Now the works of the flesh are plain”? For if, as you have shown, the whole body becomes an instrument of truth, of the wisdom and goodness of God, why does Paul disparage the flesh? By “flesh” he means the fleshly mind: gratifying the flesh alone and not caring for the soul, providing for present things and neglecting the things to come. For when someone indulges in luxury and busies himself with the adornment of the body, so as to pamper the body while his soul is ulcerated with countless wounds, then he is fleshly, since he is devoted to the flesh and pays no attention to the soul. And to show that by “flesh” he means the fleshly mind, Paul says to the faithful: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit.” Were the people he was writing to without flesh, then? The heretics do not know the idioms of the Scriptures; they do not understand how Scripture hangs together. If the flesh is alien to God, why did God say, “It shall come to pass in the last days that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh”? Why not on every soul? Why not on every mind, but on all flesh? If the flesh is alien to God, why does David say, “To you all flesh shall come”?

But Scripture often calls the whole human being “flesh,” naming it from a part. Often it also calls the same human being “soul,” naming the whole from a part. And often it calls the whole human being “breath.” When it wishes to call a human being “flesh,” then, it names not only the body but also the soul, as we said a moment ago: “To you all flesh shall come,” that is, every human being. For flesh by itself, without soul or mind, is not what is being proclaimed. When, again, it wishes to designate the whole human being by the soul, it says: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy-five souls.” Clearly those who went down into Egypt were not bodiless souls but complete human beings. And at times the divine Scripture calls the whole human being “breath,” as in: “Let every breath praise the Lord.” And not only here, but also when King Jehu was slaying his enemies, the book of Kings says: “And King Jehu struck down the house of Ahab, and no breath was left in his house,” that is, no human being was left. So Scripture speaks of the flesh in one way when it proclaims our nature, and in another way when it rebukes the fleshly mind.

But let us return to our subject. “Now the works of the flesh are plain” — not of the visible flesh, but of the fleshly mind. And so that you may learn that he is disparaging not this flesh of ours but the undisciplined mind, listen to him as he lists the deeds: “Now the works of the flesh are plain: they are fornication, adultery, idolatry.” Granted that fornication belongs to the body, and adultery to the body: is idolatry a work of the body, or a practice of the soul? “The works of the flesh are plain: they are fornication, adultery.” Are only these of the flesh, or also “idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, selfish rivalries, dissensions”? All these are foreign to the body and proper to the soul — proper to the soul, I mean, not by nature but by free choice. Indeed, if one pays close attention, one finds the heretics’ definition turned back against themselves.

They say that the soul belongs to God but the flesh to the devil. Yet we find from Scripture that the flesh is counted worthy of the Holy Spirit, while the soul does not receive the things of the Spirit. I am speaking here of the wording, not saying that the soul is never counted worthy; I am opposing the heretics' argument. If the flesh is foreign to God, how did God say, “I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh”? If the soul is God's own work, why does the natural man, the man of the soul, not receive the things of the Spirit? It has therefore been clearly shown that the works of the flesh do not belong to the body, but to the fleshly mind. Paul explains this elsewhere too, when he says, “The mind of the flesh is hostile to God.” It is not the flesh that is hostile, but the mind of the flesh. Have you learned what “flesh” means? Hold this definition firm. And when Paul says that “flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God,” understand, he means, that the mind of the flesh does not inherit the kingdom of God. For the flesh is not excluded from the inheritance. It is those who deny the resurrection who make use of this saying.

“How,” he says, “can you say that the flesh is raised, when Paul says, ‘Flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God’?” Flesh, that is, the fleshly mind, does not inherit the kingdom; in other words, whoever thinks wicked things is a stranger to the kingdom. That is why the apostle, wishing elsewhere to explain what “Flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God” means, says in his letter to the Corinthians: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with men, nor drunkards, nor revilers will inherit the kingdom of God.” So when Paul often speaks of the flesh, he is not disparaging the visible form, but the fleshly mind. And how can the flesh be evil when it was counted worthy to become the temple of God the Word? Why would the Good One take up a work that was foreign to him, if what he had fashioned were not his own? Why does he take up what is foreign? Why does he set right what is foreign? Why does he heal the blind, and not let wickedness go lame? Wickedness, when blind, is powerless and shown to be weak. Let it stay weak! Why strengthen its instruments? But the creation is not foreign to him. Hear him say to the Pharisees: “Have you not read that he who made them made them male and female?” Male and female is not a shaping of souls, but of bodies.

These things also refute the heretics who bring a new drama before us, I mean the followers of Apollinaris, who say that the Savior took on an ensouled body without the mind. Listen to how they put it, for perhaps you do not know the new drama of this heresy. What do I mean? What do the heretics say? I do not come to this inquiry without reason. It is because a great uproar has been stirred up by certain people against the faith, as though they held right views and the Church were limping in the faith. So it is necessary to lay bare both the absurdity of that newly invented impiety and the steadfastness of the faith that does not shake the apostolic rule. The heretics say that God the Word took on an ensouled body without the mind. And if you ask them why he did not take on the mind, they say: “Because the first creation was corrupted and the devil deceived man, and man was deceived by surrendering his own mind to the devil; so he did not take it, lest it muddy the plan of salvation.” I do not know whether the listeners have not already condemned the heretics before the examination, but even so, let us test the question.

The heretics say that the Savior became man without the mind, and as evidence for their own view they drag in that saying of the Gospel, “The Word became flesh.” “It did not say,” he says, “that the Word became man, but flesh.” But it has been shown from what was said earlier that “flesh” in general signifies man: “To you all flesh shall come.” But let us ask why he did not take on the mind. “So that it would not hinder salvation.” So then, was he afraid of the mind, as being stronger and able to hinder the plan of salvation? If God the Word himself declined the mind, why am I judged? Why did he bind up with me so great an evil, which he himself declined? And why does he judge me for the sins I have committed?

But see another piece of their folly. “If there were the Word of God and a human mind,” he says, “there would be a battle.” But battles arise between equals, not between the lesser and the superior. If they said that the nature of the mind was equal in rank to the power of God the Word, they would rightly be bringing forward this equality, so that it would not cause strife. But if the one is God and the other a human faculty of thought, why do you cast out the mind? “So that it would not rebel,” he says, “against the plan of salvation.” Is there anything stronger than God? Is there anything that overcomes and limits his will? Paul overcame the mind—Paul, admittedly an ordinary man, admittedly having a human mind—and he says, “But we have the mind of Christ,” as though the human mind had been put to death and changed into a divine mind. And in Paul and the apostles the mind that thinks evil things was put to death and one mind took the place of another, yet in the divine body it was going to rebel against the Creator of nature? I remind those who know these things, and I speak to those who know, so that no one may unwittingly take in the venom of the heresy, and none of the simple may give up their ears to the deception.

“He did not take on the mind,” he says. Why? “Because it would have distorted and muddied the plan of salvation.” Then why did he take on this flesh too? For Paul does not say that sins are the works of the mind; he ascribed all sin to the flesh, not to the mind. “For the works of the flesh are plain,” he says, “which are fornication, adultery,” and the rest. Why then did he take on sinful flesh, if the flesh is opposed to the Spirit? For what reason did he take on what is opposed? But, you say, he quenched the resistance of the flesh and made it be still. Then did he not likewise make the mind be still? What folly, man! Wine changes the mind; does God not change the mind? But let the folly be laughed at, and let the things of God be proclaimed. There was, then, in the Savior's flesh the human mind, but it did not think human thoughts, just as the flesh did not either. The flesh was human, yet it surpassed human limits by the power that is above the world.

And so that I may hand you a clear and unconfused picture, take, I beg you, the proofs of what has been said with patience. In the flesh there are passions that lie outside sin, and there are passions that lie within sin. Likewise in the soul there are passions outside sin, and passions within sin. What do I mean? Passions of the flesh outside sin are hunger, thirst, and sleep. These are passions, but not of sin; they belong to the weakness of the flesh: hunger, thirst, sleep, growing weary from walking, and many other things akin to these. But there are other passions of the flesh: licentiousness, a lustful eye that looks wickedly and pries into other people's faces, a tongue that utters deceit, hands stretched out to do violence. These are works of sin. We shall find, then, that the Savior, in the flesh, was wholly and entirely above the passions that lead to sin, but came within the passions that show weakness, for the sake of the plan of salvation. For he hungered: “having fasted forty days, he was afterward hungry.” And being thirsty he asked the Samaritan woman for water, and having traveled he grew weary from the journey. The nature that knows no weariness grew weary; he who feeds all hungered; he who waters the world thirsted; he who lulls the waves to sleep slept. He displayed all the passions of the flesh, apart from sin. But the passions that lie within sin he did not commit, he of whom it is said, “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

You have seen him share in the passions of the flesh that are outside sin. Now see him share in the passions of the soul that are outside sin. Passions of the soul that are reckoned as sin are evil thoughts and shameful imaginings. These are passions of a soul that inclines toward sin by its own free choice. But the soul has other passions that are outside sin: grief, timidity, and fear. No one was ever condemned for being timid; no one was rejected for fear; no one was dishonored for grief. For these are common passions of nature, and the passions of the soul that are outside sin are blameless. Just as he shared [?] in the passions of the flesh that are outside sin, so he also shared in the passions of the soul that are outside sin. Hear him say: “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death,” and again, “My soul is troubled.” Trouble is the working of fear. The flesh, the human vessel, was afraid. It was afraid of the experience of death. He himself makes the distinction and clearly shows that it was not the divine Spirit that was timid, but the flesh that recognized its own weakness: “The spirit,” he says, “is willing, but the flesh is weak.” He grieved and was troubled.

Here pay close attention, you who say that there was no human mind in the Savior's flesh. He himself said that he both grieved and was troubled. Either grant the mind that is by nature troubled and grieved, or, if you cast it out and bring in God in place of the reasoning faculty, you attach these passions to God. For what is he saying? That without the mind the soul grieves and fears and is troubled? That is impossible. And I offer the proof from experience itself. Infants admittedly have both soul and body. The mind is present in them, but it has not yet become distinct. It exists, but it has not yet received its proper activity. And just as the tongue is born together with the child at once, yet the child has not yet received speech from nature, but the tongue is an instrument of speech and has no speech, so too the mind is implanted in the soul at once, but does not at once receive its activity. As time goes on, the mind is awakened and the tongue is trained. So while infants are in the condition of childhood and have not yet received a discerning mind, but have it lulled to sleep by inexperience and resting in simplicity, until then they neither fear what ought to be feared nor grieve over what ought to be grieved over; and even if they grieve or rejoice, both their grief and their gladness are without reasoning.

What do I mean? An infant can laugh on a day of mourning while others weep; it can ask for bread while everyone mourns. For it does not [?] reckon with what lies before it. It sees its father dead and does not reckon the calamity. It sees its mother laid out and is not struck by the grief that has befallen it; its simplicity leads it into freedom from care, and in mourning it is not troubled but laughs. And on the road, often, when robbers attack and bare their swords and everyone is in terror, the infant is not troubled, for it has no experience of sword and blood and murder. When it sees a snake it is not alarmed. It sees fire and is not afraid, but delights in its brightness and often puts its hand into the fire. Have you never seen an infant reach out its hand to the lamp, attending to its brightness and not considering its power to burn? And just as distressing things do not trouble it, so neither do bright things rouse it to gladness. An infant can cry and wail and complain on a wedding day, and, being without reasoning, shares neither in the joy nor in the grief. Since, then, you cast the mind out of the human vessel that the Savior took on, either give me this mind that grieves, or, by casting it out, you plainly bring in a Godhead that grieves and is troubled.

I would have prayed that none of you should hear either their teachings or the explanations about them, for I did not want you to see either the wound or the plaster for the wound. But since the sore is spreading, and under the guise of orthodoxy it brings in false doctrine and says that Christ did not take on a mind, and makes innovations against the apostolic teachings, we have of necessity examined these things, so that we might both silence them and make you secure. Receive the authoritative teaching of the faith. Learn that Christ took on the whole man who had fallen, and that he restored [?] the whole nature that had been undone. Did the flesh alone sin? Did the soul alone sin? Was the mind alone a stranger to sin? If the mind had no share in sin, it would not have needed healing either. “For those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” But if the mind too had a share in sin, why do you bring in a partial healing? The soul sinned and needed healing. Indeed it is written: “The soul that sins shall die.” And see the precision: the sin that Scripture ascribed here to the soul, it elsewhere reckons to the flesh, accusing flesh and understanding together, so that no one might think that the flesh is in itself an evil creation, while the mind is a stranger to the flesh and free of sins. The inspired apostle declares it clearly, saying something like this: “And we were by nature children of wrath, doing the wishes of the flesh and of the thoughts,” in order to show clearly that soul and body and mind all sinned. And that it is not the flesh alone that suffers corruption, but the mind too, he says again elsewhere: “Men corrupted in mind.” If, then, the flesh sinned and the soul sinned and the mind was corrupted, and the whole vessel was corrupted, why would he not take on the whole?

“But if you speak of a complete man,” he says, “you have your hopes placed in a man.” I proclaim Christ as man and do not deny it—but man and God: God by his dignity, man by the plan of salvation. I call him man because of the condition visible outwardly, God because of the dignity within, dwelling in the humanity as in a temple. And I do not refuse to say “man,” since Paul did not deny it either: “For there is one mediator between God and men,” he says, “the man Jesus Christ.” And do you want to learn precisely that the Lord calls himself Son of Man? Hear him say: “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” If he did not truly take on the image of man which the devil had corrupted, why does he call a half-man “Son of Man”? And why, brother, if he did not have the mind, but the visible instrument consisted only of soul and body, why does the apostle call the Savior Adam? For if he is not complete, he is not Adam. The apostle names our Lord Jesus God because of his dignity: “Christ according to the flesh,” he says, “who is God over all, blessed.” And he calls him man because of the plan of salvation. And he names him Adam in order to show the plan of salvation: “The first man Adam,” he says, “became a living soul; the second Adam a life-giving spirit.” If he did not clothe himself with the whole Adam, why is he called Adam?

And so that you may learn again from another clear proof, brother, that the whole man was taken up through the Lord's flesh, hear Paul say: “Knowing this, that our old man was crucified.” If it was not the whole man, why does he call him the old man? But let this suffice against the heretics. Let us return to our own nobility. Our nobility is the apostolic faith, the apostolic profession. We all have the mind of Christ. But those who deny the mind are “men corrupted in mind, disqualified regarding the faith.” But so much for these things. May we, abiding by the apostolic definitions, keep our praise of God undefiled, wall off our ears from the heretics, and know the mind of the Church, know the profession of the faith, know the mystery of baptism, and know the dignity of the faith. And may we be counted worthy of the faith, so that as we were baptized, so we may also believe and so give glory, offering true glory to the Father and to the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
